about: Reference list /grammatica/verbi-con-preposizioni (Italian: verbs with prepositions). items: [verb + preposition, what follows (qualcuno = somebody, qualcosa = something, inf. = infinitive), example, level]. Sorted by preposition; a section's name is the preposition itself (the worksheet and the live quiz blank it in the example, so each example must use it as the verb's preposition before any other use of the same word, must not merge it with an article (al, del), and no other preposition of this list may also be right in that gap).
title: Verbs with prepositions
metaTitle: Italian verbs with prepositions: list with examples – Reference – icanspeak Italian
description: Common Italian verbs with a fixed preposition, sorted by a, di, da, in, con, su and per: what follows each one, and an example sentence.
lead: The most common verbs with a fixed preposition, sorted by preposition. For each verb: what follows it and an example.
regel: Learn the verb and its preposition together: *pensare a, sognare di, dipendere da, contare su.*
After a preposition, a verb stays in the infinitive: *Sogno di vivere vicino al mare.*
In questions the preposition goes first: *Con chi parli? A che cosa pensi?*

Some verbs take no preposition in Italian where English has one: *aspettare l'autobus* (wait for), *cercare le chiavi* (look for), *ascoltare la radio* (listen to), *pagare il conto* (pay for), *guardare la TV* (look at).
A preposition joins with the article: *a + il = al, di + la = della, in + lo = nello.* So *Gioco a calcio* but *Parliamo del contratto.*
Some verbs take more than one preposition with a different meaning: *pensare a* (think about someone) and *pensare di* (intend to), *parlare di* (about) and *parlare con* (to).
practice: Pronouns after prepositions: a me, con te
